explain.curious: Starlight spreads out as it travels: twice as far away, a quarter of the light.
explain.science: Inverse-square law for an isotropic source. At the semi-major axis this is close to the orbit-averaged flux for low eccentricity (the exact average is larger by 1/√(1 - e²)).

f.name: how much of the sphere shares the heat

source.text: Catling, D. C. and Kasting, J. F. 2017, Atmospheric Evolution on Inhabited and Lifeless Worlds, Cambridge University Press

explain.curious: How warm a world would be if it were a bare ball that only absorbs and glows. Earth's comes out at a frozen −18 °C; the air makes up the rest.
explain.science: Balance of absorbed starlight against black-body emission. The redistribution factor sets how much of the sphere shares the absorbed heat.

equation.name: How warm the ground is under a heat-trapping sky

tau.name: how opaque the air is to heat (infrared optical depth)

source.text: Pierrehumbert, R. T. 2010, Principles of Planetary Climate, Cambridge University Press

explain.curious: Air that lets sunlight in but holds heat back keeps the ground warmer than the bare-ball figure. The thicker that blanket, the warmer.
explain.science: Grey radiative-equilibrium atmosphere in the Eddington approximation, with all sunlight absorbed at the ground and one infrared optical depth τ. Earth needs τ ≈ 0.87 (0.83 with T_eq = 255 K); Venus about 140 (737 K over T_eq ≈ 230 K). It ignores convection, which in reality caps the lapse rate, so it overstates hot thick atmospheres.
